transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Honestly, I'm here because... well, it's getting to be a bit of a professional liability, and a personal one too, if I'm being completely honest. The main thing that brings me in is that I just keep getting up when I am really, absolutely supposed to stay put. 

Like, I'm a private investigator, right? So a huge part of my job is sitting across from clients and just listening to them lay out these incredibly sensitive, complicated situations. But I just can't stay in my chair. I'll be in the middle of a serious client interview, and they're pouring their heart out about a cheating spouse or a missing business asset, and I just stand up. I start pacing, or I walk over to the window, or I pretend I need to adjust the blinds. 

And it's not just at work, which is the frustrating part! I do some tutoring on the side—mostly high school kids—and I'll just wander away from the desk while the poor kid is trying to work through a practice test. Or even my book club! We meet on Thursday nights, and last week we were discussing this really dense mystery novel, and I must have gotten up from the sofa five or six times in half an hour. I went to the kitchen, I fixed a throw pillow, I watered a plant that wasn't even mine. 

People are really starting to notice, and that's why I made the appointment. My clients look at me like I don't care about their cases, and the women at book club actually stopped the discussion to ask if I was feeling okay because it's become so obvious that I just can't sit and listen. It's incredibly embarrassing. I just feel like sitting in a chair is suddenly the most impossible task in the world, and I don't know why I can't just stay seated like everyone else in the room.
Do you feel anxious or uneasy when you are forced to stay seated and can't get up?

Anxious? Hmm. No, I really wouldn't use the word anxious. It’s not like a worry or a panic, or like I’m scared something bad is going to happen if I don't get up. It’s definitely not an emotional uneasiness. 

It’s more like... well, for example, I was at this deposition a few weeks ago for a corporate embezzlement case I’ve been working on—which, by the way, is a fascinating case, lots of hidden offshore accounts and shell companies—but anyway, I was sitting there in this very stuffy conference room with all these lawyers, and I was completely calm mentally. I wasn't stressed or uneasy at all. I was actually really interested in what the witness was saying. But after about twenty minutes, it was like my body just decided, completely on its own, that it was time to be vertical. 

It’s almost like a physical pressure, like a spring being pressed down, and it just has to release. I don't get a racing heart or a nervous stomach or anything like that. I don't feel that claustrophobic panic some people get. I just suddenly feel this overwhelming, purely physical pull to stand up. It’s not a feeling of dread or anxiety in the slightest. I can be totally engaged in the conversation, perfectly happy, completely fine, and then I just find myself standing up before I've even consciously decided to do it. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel anxious or uneasy when I'm stuck in a chair... my body just refuses to stay in it.
Do you find it hard to focus on what's being discussed when you're sitting?

Focus? No, not really. I mean, it's not like my mind is wandering off or anything like that. Actually, I'm usually hyper-focused on what's being said, especially if it's a client interview or a deposition. I remember this one time, just last month, I was sitting with this woman who suspected her husband of hiding assets before a divorce—which is incredibly common, by the way, you'd be amazed at the lengths people go to, setting up trusts in their mother's maiden name, buying expensive art and keeping it in storage—anyway, she was going through all these financial records she'd found, and I was tracking every single word. I was completely dialed in. I wasn't distracted at all. I was processing the dates, the amounts, cross-referencing them in my head with the standard practices for forensic accounting. I was totally there, mentally. 

But at the same time, my legs were just... bouncing. And then I was standing up, walking over to the white board in my office, even though I didn't need to write anything down. I was still listening to her, still asking relevant questions, still completely engaged in the conversation. It's just that my body was moving while my brain was working. So it's definitely not a focus issue. It's not like I'm sitting there daydreaming about what I'm going to have for dinner or losing the thread of the conversation. I hear everything, I understand everything, I'm right there with them. I just... I just can't do it while my bottom is glued to a chair. It's like the physical movement and the mental focus are completely separate systems, and the mental one is working perfectly fine, but the physical one is just constantly hitting the 'go' button. Does that make sense? Because sometimes I feel like I'm explaining it poorly, but it's just so strange to be completely mentally present but physically unable to stay still.
Do you feel any relief when you finally get up and move around after being seated for a while?

Relief? Gosh, I don't know if I'd call it relief, exactly. It's not like taking off a tight pair of shoes at the end of the day, you know? It's not that kind of "ahhh" feeling. I mean, I guess I've never really thought about it in terms of feeling relieved. 

It's more just... I don't know, it's just what happens. Like last week, I was doing this stakeout—which, by the way, stakeouts are not nearly as glamorous as they look on television, it's mostly just sitting in a hot car eating lukewarm takeout and trying not to spill coffee on yourself—but I was sitting there for maybe two hours, and I just had to get out of the car. I didn't feel relieved when I stepped out onto the pavement, I just felt like I was finally doing what my body had been trying to do for the last hour. 

And then, of course, I had to pretend I was just stretching my legs or checking a tire, because you can't just be pacing around outside a suspect's house, that defeats the whole purpose of a stakeout. But even then, walking around the car, it wasn't a feeling of relief. It was just... movement. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel relief. I just don't really notice a specific feeling of relief when I get up, it's just more that the pressure to move is temporarily satisfied, I suppose. I don't know if that answers your question, but I just haven't really experienced it as a sense of relief. It's just so automatic at this point.
Do you have difficulty completing tasks that require sustained mental effort over a long period?

Sustained mental effort? Oh, no. No, definitely not. If anything, it's the exact opposite. I mean, in my line of work, you absolutely have to have incredible mental stamina, and I've never had a problem with it. 

People think being a private investigator is all car chases and confronting bad guys in dark alleys, but honestly, ninety percent of it is incredibly tedious, complex, puzzle-solving work that takes hours and hours of brainpower. Take background checks, for example. A real, comprehensive background investigation—especially for high-net-worth clients or corporate mergers, which is a lot of what I do—isn't just typing a name into a database. It's grueling. 

Just a few days ago, I was looking into this potential CEO candidate for a mid-sized tech firm. I had to pull property records across four different states, cross-reference them with civil litigation databases, check for undisclosed liens... and you wouldn't believe how often people try to hide bankruptcies by slightly altering their middle initial or using a variation of their surname. It's shockingly common. Anyway, I was working on this file, and I was mentally locked in for about seven or eight hours straight. I didn't lose my train of thought once. I traced this guy's entire financial history back to 1998, found a messy little breach of contract lawsuit he'd tried to bury, and wrote up a forty-page dossier. 

The mental effort part of it is totally fine for me. I can grind through thousands of pages of legal discovery, I can analyze hours of grainy security footage looking for a two-second discrepancy, I can read through endless strings of corporate emails to establish a timeline... I can do all of that without any mental fatigue or difficulty finishing the job. I always get it done. My brain doesn't get tired or just give up on the hard stuff. Now, like I was saying before, was I sitting perfectly still at my desk while I did all this? Of course not. I was pacing around my home office with my tablet, standing at the kitchen counter, shifting my weight from one foot to the other. But mentally? The mental endurance is absolutely there. I don't struggle to complete those long, complicated tasks at all.
Do you ever feel like you need to do something in a very specific way or repeat certain actions?

Specific ways? Repeat actions? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I don't have any kind of rituals or compulsions or anything like that, if that's what you're asking. I don't need to tap the doorframe three times before I leave a room or organize my desk in a perfectly symmetrical way. 

I mean, as an investigator, I have procedures, obviously. I have a very specific methodology for how I log evidence, how I document my hours, how I back up my digital files. You have to, right? Because if you don't follow the chain of custody perfectly, or if your notes are sloppy, a defense attorney will tear you apart on the stand. I've seen it happen to other PIs, and it's brutal. They get up there, they stutter, they can't remember if they took a photo at 2:00 PM or 2:15 PM, and suddenly their entire testimony is thrown out. So, yes, I am very meticulous about my work processes. When I'm doing a surveillance log, I use the exact same format every single time: date, time, location, weather conditions, subject description, activity. I never deviate from that. 

But that's professional necessity, not some kind of personal need to repeat things. In my personal life? Heavens, no. I'm actually pretty flexible. I don't care if the dishwasher is loaded a certain way, I don't have a rigid morning routine that I have to follow or else my whole day is ruined. I just kind of roll with things. So, no, I don't feel a need to do things in a very specific way or repeat actions, outside of just doing my job correctly and thoroughly. It's not a... it's not a compulsion or anything. It's just standard operating procedure for a private detective.
Do you often act on impulse without fully thinking through the consequences?

Act on impulse? Oh, definitely not. No, I really don't do that. I mean, if I just acted without thinking through the consequences, I wouldn't have a license anymore. 

In my line of work, you have to be ten steps ahead at all times. You have to think about the legal ramifications of every single move you make. If I'm on a surveillance job—say, a domestic case, which I honestly try not to take as much anymore because they're just so emotionally exhausting and messy, but occasionally I'll take one if the retainer is right—but if I see the subject walk into a restaurant with someone who clearly isn't their spouse, an impulsive person might just barge right in there, right? Just run in to try and get the money shot up close before they leave. 

But you absolutely cannot do that. You have to sit there and calculate. You have to ask yourself, is this a public space where they have no reasonable expectation of privacy? Am I going to get made if I walk in? What's my cover story if the maître d' stops me and asks if I have a reservation? Do I have the right lens on my camera to just shoot through the window from across the street instead, which is infinitely safer? You have to weigh all those variables constantly. 

I had a workers' comp fraud case just a few months ago where the guy was claiming total disability, swore under oath he couldn't lift more than ten pounds without excruciating pain. I tracked him to a local hardware store, and he was loading eighty-pound bags of concrete into the bed of his truck. Concrete! Now, the urge to just run up and start filming right next to his bumper is there, sure, because it's the smoking gun, it's the exact thing the client is paying me to find. But if I act on that impulse, he sees me, the investigation is completely blown, and he might even get physically aggressive. People get very, very defensive when they realize they're being caught in a massive lie. 

So I had to think it all through. I positioned my vehicle across the lot, angled it so I had a clear line of sight but looked like I was just parking, used a telephoto lens, made sure his face, the concrete bags, and his license plate were all in the same frame... it's all incredibly calculated. I always think about what's going to happen next. I have to, or I'd be out of a job and probably facing a harassment lawsuit. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive like that at all. I always think through the consequences.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting with your hands or feet when you're sitting still?

Fidgeting? Oh, absolutely. That’s... well, like I mentioned earlier about pacing, sitting actually still is pretty much impossible for me. If I’m forced to be planted in my chair—like when I’m stuck at the computer combing through hundreds of pages of digital records, which happens a lot when I'm running deep-web searches or pulling municipal court dockets—my body just will not stay quiet. 

My foot is constantly bouncing under the desk. Just... a mile a minute, like a jackhammer. Half the time I don’t even realize I’m doing it until my knee bangs into the keyboard tray or the monitor actually starts vibrating on the stand. 

And my hands, oh my goodness. If there is a pen anywhere within reaching distance, I am clicking it. I always buy those retractable gel pens—the fine point ones, because they're the best for taking notes on the back of glossy photo paper without smudging—and I will just sit there and click, click, click it while I read. I don't even know I'm doing it until it starts echoing in the room and I annoy myself. 

And it's not even just the hands and feet, it's my whole posture. I'm constantly shifting around in the seat. I’ll cross my left leg over my right, then five seconds later I’ll swap them, then I’ll pull one knee up to my chest, then I'll lean all the way back. Honestly, I shift around so much that I actually lose my place in what I'm reading. Which, let me tell you, is incredibly frustrating when you're staring at a densely packed Excel spreadsheet of some guy's hidden offshore bank transactions. Mentally, I know exactly what I'm looking for, but physically, I move so much that my eyes jump down three rows and I have to trace my finger back up the screen to find the line I was just on. So, yes, if I have to sit still, my hands and feet are absolutely going non-stop.
Do you ever feel the need to move or be active when you're not sitting, such as when you're standing or in other positions?

Oh, constantly. It’s like... well, if sitting is hard, standing around doing nothing is just as bad, if not worse. It’s like I have this internal engine that just doesn't have an off switch. 

Even on days when I don't have field work—which, honestly, are supposed to be my catch-up days, the days I stay at the home office and maybe just take a breath—I can never actually do that. I just keep moving. I’ll be up on my feet, and suddenly I’m unpacking boxes of old archived records that I haven't needed in three years. I'll pull everything out, and then halfway through that, I'll move over to the filing cabinets and start completely reorganizing my active case files. I’ll pull them all out, spread them across the counter, and just speed-walk back and forth across the room sorting them by priority and date. 

And then, if the office feels too small and I've run out of things to shuffle around, I have to get out, so I'll start running errands. But I don't just run errands like a normal person taking a leisurely stroll through the grocery store. No, I am darting from the post office to the bank to the hardware store like I'm actively chasing a lead on a hot case. I walk fast, I'm constantly scanning the room, I'm checking my watch... I treat picking up dry cleaning like I'm tailing a suspect who's about to skip town. 

I just... I have an incredibly hard time just being off duty. You know? People talk about unwinding on their days off, just standing in the kitchen making a cup of coffee and looking out the window, but I can't do that. If I'm standing in the kitchen, I'm wiping down the counters, I'm rearranging the pantry, I'm pacing the hallway while the coffee brews. It's exhausting, honestly, but if I'm not physically tied to a chair doing research, my body just demands to be in motion, constantly, like there's a ticking clock only I can hear. So yes, I am always, always on the move.
Do you think you might be moving around so much as a way to avoid thinking about something unpleasant or dealing with difficult emotions?

Avoid difficult emotions? Huh. I... no, I really don't think that's it. I mean, I get why you'd ask that, because sure, my line of work is basically a front-row seat to people's worst days. You see a lot of unpleasant things. Just last month I had to hand over a file to a woman proving her husband of twenty years was living a completely double life in the next county over, complete with a second mortgage. That’s heavy, right? It’s messy. And you’d think maybe I pace around my office to shake that kind of thing off, or to avoid thinking about the look on her face when she saw the surveillance photos. 

But honestly? That’s not it at all. Because I do the exact same thing when I'm perfectly fine. I do it when I'm happy! If I just closed a massive corporate espionage case, the client is thrilled, the invoice is paid in full, there is zero emotional baggage or stress whatsoever... I'm still pacing the exact same way. I'm still pulling out old boxes and reorganizing the filing cabinets. I'm still practically jogging through the grocery store aisles when I go to pick up dinner. 

It’s not... it doesn't feel like I'm running away from a thought, if that makes sense? It's not a distraction tactic. It just feels like my body has this excess electricity. Like a battery that’s been overcharged, and if I don't burn it off by physically moving my limbs, my skin is just going to crawl. It's like the physical movement has absolutely nothing to do with my emotional state. It's just this constant, humming motor. So, no, I really wouldn't say it's an emotional avoidance thing at all. It's just how my body operates, whether it's a good day or a bad day.
Do you have trouble sleeping or find that you sleep more or less than you think you should?

Sleep? No, actually, sleep is... well, it’s probably the one time my brain and my body actually shut off, to be completely honest. 

I mean, my schedule is completely erratic, obviously. You can't really work a strict nine-to-five when you're a private investigator. Sometimes I’m sitting in my car outside a sketchy motel out on Route 9 until three in the morning, waiting to get a time-stamped photo of a subject for a client, so I won't even get back to my house and get into bed until four or four-thirty. But that’s just the nature of the job, that’s not me having trouble sleeping. 

When my head actually hits the pillow, I am out cold. I don't toss and turn, I don't stare at the ceiling worrying about things. I think because I'm burning so much physical and mental energy during the day—you know, with all the pacing I mentioned, the constant moving, running around town, and staring at screens—by the time I actually decide it's time to go to sleep, my battery is just completely empty. 

And I usually get a solid seven or eight hours, too. Even if I go to bed at 4 AM, I've got these heavy, industrial-grade blackout curtains installed in my bedroom. I actually tracked down the commercial supplier that provides them for high-end hotel chains, because the standard ones you buy at a regular department store always let that little sliver of daylight in on the sides, and I just couldn't have that. So my room is pitch black, and I just sleep right through until noon if I need to. I don't wake up feeling groggy or exhausted, and I don't oversleep and stay in bed for twelve hours either. It's just a perfectly normal amount of sleep. It just happens on a slightly shifted timeline depending on my active caseload. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I have any trouble in the sleep department whatsoever. People always assume I have insomnia because I'll send them case updates at two in the morning, but I'm just working! When I actually go to sleep, I sleep great. It's pretty much the only time I'm actually sitting still.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others or finishing their sentences for them?

Oh, absolutely. It's... well, it's actually a bit of a running joke at the agency, though honestly, I'm sure it's probably more annoying to people than they let on. I just can't seem to help it. 

If I'm walking through the office and I hear a couple of the junior detectives discussing a lead on a case—even if it has absolutely nothing to do with me, even if I'm supposed to be heading out the door to meet a client—I just physically cannot keep walking. My brain hears a puzzle or a situation and it just latches on. Before I even know what I'm doing, I've stopped at their desks and I'm jumping right in with a dozen questions. I'll start firing off advice, telling them how they need to run the background check, or who they should interview next, or where to position the surveillance vehicle, completely unprompted. They didn't ask for my help! They were just bouncing ideas off each other. And it's only afterward, when I'm finally walking away, that it hits me and I realize I completely barged into someone else's conversation and just hijacked the whole thing. 

And it's not even just a professional hazard, it happens everywhere. It's like I have zero boundary between hearing words and participating in them. Just the other day I was walking down the hallway in my apartment building to check my mail, and two of my neighbors were talking by the elevator. I don't even know them that well, you know, just a polite nod here and there. But I overheard them talking about a dispute with the building manager, and suddenly I'm right there in the middle of it. I'm giving them advice on how to document the correspondence, asking them specific questions about the clauses in their lease agreement... before they even looked at me or asked me a single thing. I just completely inserted myself. 

And then the elevator doors open, they get in looking a little bewildered, and I'm just standing there by the mailboxes thinking, "Why did I just do that?" I just... my mouth moves so fast. I hear people talking and I just jump right in with my two cents before I realize I wasn't actually invited to the discussion.
Do you ever feel like you can truly relax and be still, without the urge to move or engage in activity?

Relax? Be still? Oh, wow. Um. No. I don't think I've actually done that since... well, maybe ever. I really don't know how people just sit and do nothing. Even on days when I don't have any field work—like, let's say it's a Sunday, the agency is closed, I have no active surveillance, no clients breathing down my neck—I still can't just be off duty. It’s like my body didn't get the memo that we have the day off. 

I'll wake up and immediately start finding things to tackle. I'll start unpacking these old banker boxes of archives that have been sitting in my spare room for months, going through old receipts and surveillance logs. And then before I even finish that, I'm pulling out current case files and completely reorganizing them. I'll color-code them, cross-reference the index tabs, completely overhauling the filing system for no immediate reason other than the fact that my hands need to be moving. 

And then I'll decide I need to run errands, right? But I don't just stroll through my errands like a normal person enjoying a weekend. I'm hitting the dry cleaners, the post office, the grocery store, and I'm doing it with this intense, driving energy. I'm practically power-walking from my car to the automatic doors, scanning the parking lot, mapping out the absolute most efficient route through the aisles like I'm actively chasing a lead on a suspect. It’s exactly the same physical intensity and momentum I have when I'm on the clock, but I'm just buying coffee filters and picking up my suits. 

I just have a really, really hard time being off duty. The concept of just sitting in a chair, maybe reading a book or watching a movie, and actually relaxing without the urge to get up and engage in some kind of project or activity... it just doesn't compute for me. If I try to just sit still, within three minutes I'm thinking about the grout in the bathroom tile or the oil change I need to get next week, and I'm back on my feet again. I always, always have to be in motion.
Are your symptoms interfering with your ability to maintain relationships or perform daily tasks?

Interfering? Well... yeah. I mean, I try to brush it off and make a joke out of it, like I mentioned with the office stuff, but if I'm really sitting down and looking at it... it's starting to cost me professionally. And in this line of work, your reputation is basically your entire currency, so it's not something I can just ignore anymore. 

For one thing, I've actually started missing details in my investigations. And I am a senior investigator, I have been doing this for over two decades, so making rookie mistakes is just incredibly frustrating. But just last month, I was running a pretty standard corporate asset search, and my brain was just moving a million miles an hour, already jumping ahead to how I was going to set up the physical surveillance, that I completely glossed over a secondary LLC tied to the subject's spouse. I just skipped right past it on the background report because I was rushing. My boss had to catch it during the review, and it was humiliating. If he hadn't caught it, we would have given the client an incomplete file. 

And speaking of the clients, I've definitely irritated more than a few of them lately. When people come to us, they're usually stressed, they're dealing with fraud or infidelity, and they want to sit in the conference room and tell their whole emotional story. But I usually get the gist of what they need in the first three minutes, and I just... I start cutting them off. I finish their sentences, I jump straight into tactical planning and retainer fees, and I can literally see their faces tighten up. They think I'm being insensitive or that I don't care, but I'm just already solving the case in my head! But it doesn't matter what my intentions are, it rubs them the wrong way. We actually had a client ask to be reassigned to a different investigator last week because she said I was too abrasive and wouldn't listen to her. 

And then there's the junior detectives. You know how I said it was a running joke that I interrupt them? Well, it turns out it's not actually that funny to them. I've started noticing that they are actively avoiding me. I used to be the one they'd come to for advice on difficult cases, but now, if they see me coming down the hall, they'll literally duck into the breakroom or suddenly get very busy looking at their phones. I actually cornered our office manager about it the other day, and she told me—off the record, of course—that the younger detectives are less willing to debrief with me now because they feel completely steamrolled. They feel like they can't even get a word in edgewise to explain their own case theories before I've completely taken over and barked a bunch of orders at them. 

It really stings, you know? Because I'm genuinely just trying to help, I just have all this momentum and I want to fix the problem for them, but it's alienating the people I work with. I'm pushing clients away, I'm making my coworkers feel small, and I'm dropping the ball on my own files. So, yeah... I guess it really is interfering. It's becoming a real problem.
Have you ever been diagnosed with or suspected to have Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, or do you have a family history of it?

Diagnosed? No. No, definitely not. I mean... I'm forty-nine years old, you know? When I was growing up, back in the late seventies and eighties, they really weren't looking for... well, whatever this is... in little girls. Unless you were a boy literally climbing the chalkboards and throwing erasers, you just flew under the radar. My teachers just wrote things on my report cards like "highly enthusiastic" or "needs to learn to wait her turn" or "a bit of a chatterbox." My parents just thought I was a tomboy with a lot of energy who liked to get into things. So no, nobody ever pulled my folks aside and suggested there was an actual medical reason for why I couldn't sit still through a single family dinner. It just wasn't something people talked about back then, especially not for girls who were otherwise doing okay.

And as for a family history... well, if anyone in my family had anything like this, they certainly never got an official label for it. We weren't really a "go to the doctor to talk about your brain" kind of family anyway. You just kept busy and got to work. 

Though, honestly, if I really sit back and think about it... my dad was a lot like me. He was a general contractor, and he was just always, always moving. He'd be juggling fifteen different job sites, talking a mile a minute to the subcontractors, constantly pacing. If my mom ever tried to make him sit down and watch a movie with us on a Friday night, he'd be up pacing the back of the living room by the second act, or suddenly deciding he needed to go reorganize the garage at nine o'clock at night. But he was never diagnosed with anything! He was just... you know, considered a "hard worker" with a lot of drive. That's just how we all framed it. 

So, officially? No. No history on paper, no past diagnoses for me. This is all completely new territory, which is probably why it's so incredibly frustrating trying to unpack it all now at this stage in my career. I've just always thought this was just who I am, just my personality, you know?
Do you often find yourself easily distracted by things around you?

Distracted? By things around me? Um... no, actually. I don't think so. I know it probably seems like I would be, right? Because I'm always moving and my engine is always running hot, people probably look at me and assume my brain is just bouncing around like a pinball machine, just pinging off of every little thing in the room. But it's really not like that at all. 

If anything, it's the exact opposite. When I am locked onto something, I am completely locked in. Take surveillance, for example. I can be sitting in an unmarked car for six hours straight—and yeah, okay, I might be tapping my foot the entire time, or aggressively chewing a piece of gum, or drumming my fingers on the steering wheel until my knuckles ache—but my eyes do not leave the front door of the target's house. A dog could run by, a fire engine could come screaming down the next block with its sirens blaring, the neighbor could come out and start weed-whacking right next to my bumper... and it doesn't pull me away. I mean, I register that it's happening, obviously, because situational awareness is literally what they pay me for, but it doesn't derail me. I don't suddenly forget why I'm there and start watching the guy do his yard work. 

Even back at the office, it's the same thing. If I'm tearing through those banker boxes I mentioned earlier, or if I'm drafting up a final case report for a client, the phone could be ringing off the hook, the junior detectives could be arguing about lunch orders right outside my door, the copier could be jamming and beeping that annoying high-pitched error tone, and I just tune it all out completely. I just zero in on whatever project I've decided needs my attention right that second. 

So no, I wouldn't say I get distracted easily. It's more like... I have this incredibly intense, laser-like focus, but the laser just happens to be attached to a motor that absolutely refuses to shut off, if that makes sense? Like, my body always has to be doing something, I always have to have that forward momentum, but whatever task I'm actually tackling, I am completely and totally consumed by it. I don't lose my train of thought just because a bird flew past the window or someone dropped a pen. Honestly, my ex-husband used to joke that a bomb could go off in the living room and I'd just complain that it got dust on my case files. So, no, I don't get sidetracked by my environment at all.
Have you ever had difficulty organizing tasks or activities?

Organizing? Oh, no. No, definitely not. Honestly, that’s probably the one thing holding my entire professional life together. If you saw my office—well, aside from the times I'm actively tearing through banker boxes like I mentioned earlier—my actual foundational system is completely airtight. 

You have to understand, in private investigation, especially when you're dealing with high-stakes corporate fraud or complex asset searches, if you aren't organized, you are completely dead in the water. One misplaced financial record or a gap in a surveillance log, and the whole case falls apart the second a lawyer looks at it. So I have this incredibly rigid system. Every single case gets a master binder, physical and digital. I have color-coded tabs—red for financial docs, blue for surveillance photos, yellow for witness interviews, green for background checks. 

And my schedule? My calendar is mapped out down to the fifteen-minute increment. I mean, I feel like I have to do that, right? I didn't stop to eat, I didn't stop to get a glass of water, I didn't even realize the sun had gone down until my office was completely pitch black and the only light in the room was the glow of my dual monitors. I know it's rude. I tell myself before every meeting, "Just bite your tongue, let him finish his sentence." But it's like... the words just bubble up my throat and out of my mouth before my brain can even hit the brakes. 

And it’s not just at work, either. It’s in everyday life. My friends get so annoyed with me. We'll be at dinner, and someone will be telling a story, and I’ll just jump right in the middle of it. Sometimes I’m trying to finish their sentence for them because they’re taking too long to get to the point, or sometimes they say one little thing that sparks a thought in my head, and I just have to get it out right that second, or I feel like I'll explode. I literally interrupted my sister at her own wedding rehearsal dinner. She was giving this heartfelt toast, and she paused to take a breath, and I just launched into this whole tangential story about the caterer. I still feel terrible about it. She was furious. 

And lines? Oh my god, don't even get me started on waiting in lines. The grocery store, the DMV, even just waiting for the coffee machine at the office. I can't just stand there. I'm shifting my weight, I'm sighing out loud, I'm looking at my watch, I'm checking my phone, I'm literally pacing in place. If there are more than three people in front of me at the grocery checkout, I will just abandon my cart and leave. I can't do it. The feeling of being trapped in a queue, just waiting for other people to take their turn... it makes my skin crawl. It's like every second stretches out into an hour. So, yeah, waiting my turn, whether it's to speak or to do something... it's a massive struggle. It always has been.

Sleep? No, actually, sleep is... well, it’s probably the one time my brain and my body actually shut off, to be completely honest. 

I mean, my schedule is completely erratic, obviously. You can't really work a strict nine-to-five when you're a private investigator. Sometimes I’m sitting in my car outside a sketchy motel out on Route 9 until three in the morning, waiting to get a time-stamped photo of a subject for a client, so I won't even get back to my house and get into bed until four or four-thirty. But that’s just the nature of the job, that’s not me having trouble sleeping. 

When my head actually hits the pillow, I am out cold. I don't toss and turn, I don't stare at the ceiling worrying about things. I think because I'm burning so much physical and mental energy during the day—you know, with all the pacing I mentioned, the constant moving, running around town, and staring at screens—by the time I actually decide it's time to go to sleep, my battery is just completely empty. 

And I usually get a solid seven or eight hours, too. Even if I go to bed at 4 AM, I've got these heavy, industrial-grade blackout curtains installed in my bedroom. I actually tracked down the commercial supplier that provides them for high-end hotel chains, because the standard ones you buy at a regular department store always let that little sliver of daylight in on the sides, and I just couldn't have that. So my room is pitch black, and I just sleep right through until noon if I need to. I don't wake up feeling groggy or exhausted, and I don't oversleep and stay in bed for twelve hours either. It's just a perfectly normal amount of sleep. It just happens on a slightly shifted timeline depending on my active caseload. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I have any trouble in the sleep department whatsoever. People always assume I have insomnia because I'll send them case updates at two in the morning, but I'm just working! When I actually go to sleep, I sleep great. It's pretty much the only time I'm actually sitting still.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's excessive movement is a result of an underlying issue with impulsivity
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself interrupting others or finishing their sentences for them?

target_item.name: Interrupting_Intruding
target_item.manifestation: If I hear junior detectives discussing a lead or a neighbor talking in the hallway, I jump in with questions or advice before I've been asked, and afterward I realize I barged into someone else's conversation.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. It's... well, it's actually a bit of a running joke at the agency, though honestly, I'm sure it's probably more annoying to people than they let on. I just can't seem to help it. 

If I'm walking through the office and I hear a couple of the junior detectives discussing a lead on a case—even if it has absolutely nothing to do with me, even if I'm supposed to be heading out the door to meet a client—I just physically cannot keep walking. My brain hears a puzzle or a situation and it just latches on. Before I even know what I'm doing, I've stopped at their desks and I'm jumping right in with a dozen questions. I'll start firing off advice, telling them how they need to run the background check, or who they should interview next, or where to position the surveillance vehicle, completely unprompted. They didn't ask for my help! They were just bouncing ideas off each other. And it's only afterward, when I'm finally walking away, that it hits me and I realize I completely barged into someone else's conversation and just hijacked the whole thing. 

And it's not even just a professional hazard, it happens everywhere. It's like I have zero boundary between hearing words and participating in them. Just the other day I was walking down the hallway in my apartment building to check my mail, and two of my neighbors were talking by the elevator. I don't even know them that well, you know, just a polite nod here and there. But I overheard them talking about a dispute with the building manager, and suddenly I'm right there in the middle of it. I'm giving them advice on how to document the correspondence, asking them specific questions about the clauses in their lease agreement... before they even looked at me or asked me a single thing. I just completely inserted myself. 

And then the elevator doors open, they get in looking a little bewildered, and I'm just standing there by the mailboxes thinking, "Why did I just do that?" I just... my mouth moves so fast. I hear people talking and I just jump right in with my two cents before I realize I wasn't actually invited to the discussion.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's excessive movement is a result of an inability to relax

target_item.name: Constant_Activity

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I can relax and be still without the urge to move or engage in activity, which directly relates to the symptom of being constantly 'on the go' or acting as if 'driven by a motor'.

patient.answer:
Relax? Be still? Oh, wow. Um. No. I don't think I've actually done that since... well, maybe ever. I really don't know how people just sit and do nothing. Even on days when I don't have any field work—like, let's say it's a Sunday, the agency is closed, I have no active surveillance, no clients breathing down my neck—I still can't just be off duty. It’s like my body didn't get the memo that we have the day off. 

I'll wake up and immediately start finding things to tackle. I'll start unpacking these old banker boxes of archives that have been sitting in my spare room for months, going through old receipts and surveillance logs. And then before I even finish that, I'm pulling out current case files and completely reorganizing them. I'll color-code them, cross-reference the index tabs, completely overhauling the filing system for no immediate reason other than the fact that my hands need to be moving. 

And then I'll decide I need to run errands, right? But I don't just stroll through my errands like a normal person enjoying a weekend. I'm hitting the dry cleaners, the post office, the grocery store, and I'm doing it with this intense, driving energy. I'm practically power-walking from my car to the automatic doors, scanning the parking lot, mapping out the absolute most efficient route through the aisles like I'm actively chasing a lead on a suspect. It’s exactly the same physical intensity and momentum I have when I'm on the clock, but I'm just buying coffee filters and picking up my suits. 

I just have a really, really hard time being off duty. The concept of just sitting in a chair, maybe reading a book or watching a movie, and actually relaxing without the urge to get up and engage in some kind of project or activity... it just doesn't compute for me. If I try to just sit still, within three minutes I'm thinking about the grout in the bathroom tile or the oil change I need to get next week, and I'm back on my feet again. I always, always have to be in motion.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning
doctor.question: Are your symptoms interfering with your ability to maintain relationships or perform daily tasks?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It's starting to cost me professionally—I've missed details in investigations, irritated clients, and made junior detectives less willing to debrief with me because they feel steamrolled.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms are interfering with my relationships or daily tasks, which directly addresses functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Interfering? Well... yeah. I mean, I try to brush it off and make a joke out of it, like I mentioned with the office stuff, but if I'm really sitting down and looking at it... it's starting to cost me professionally. And in this line of work, your reputation is basically your entire currency, so it's not something I can just ignore anymore. 

For one thing, I've actually started missing details in my investigations. And I am a senior investigator, I have been doing this for over two decades, so making rookie mistakes is just incredibly frustrating. But just last month, I was running a pretty standard corporate asset search, and my brain was just moving a million miles an hour, already jumping ahead to how I was going to set up the physical surveillance, that I completely glossed over a secondary LLC tied to the subject's spouse. I just skipped right past it on the background report because I was rushing. My boss had to catch it during the review, and it was humiliating. If he hadn't caught it, we would have given the client an incomplete file. 

And speaking of the clients, I've definitely irritated more than a few of them lately. When people come to us, they're usually stressed, they're dealing with fraud or infidelity, and they want to sit in the conference room and tell their whole emotional story. But I usually get the gist of what they need in the first three minutes, and I just... I start cutting them off. I finish their sentences, I jump straight into tactical planning and retainer fees, and I can literally see their faces tighten up. They think I'm being insensitive or that I don't care, but I'm just already solving the case in my head! But it doesn't matter what my intentions are, it rubs them the wrong way. We actually had a client ask to be reassigned to a different investigator last week because she said I was too abrasive and wouldn't listen to her. 

And then there's the junior detectives. You know how I said it was a running joke that I interrupt them? Well, it turns out it's not actually that funny to them. I've started noticing that they are actively avoiding me. I used to be the one they'd come to for advice on difficult cases, but now, if they see me coming down the hall, they'll literally duck into the breakroom or suddenly get very busy looking at their phones. I actually cornered our office manager about it the other day, and she told me—off the record, of course—that the younger detectives are less willing to debrief with me now because they feel completely steamrolled. They feel like they can't even get a word in edgewise to explain their own case theories before I've completely taken over and barked a bunch of orders at them. 

It really stings, you know? Because I'm genuinely just trying to help, I just have all this momentum and I want to fix the problem for them, but it's alienating the people I work with. I'm pushing clients away, I'm making my coworkers feel small, and I'm dropping the ball on my own files. So, yeah... I guess it really is interfering. It's becoming a real problem.

Diagnosed? No. No, definitely not. I mean... I'm forty-nine years old, you know? When I was growing up, back in the late seventies and eighties, they really weren't looking for... well, whatever this is... in little girls. Unless you were a boy literally climbing the chalkboards and throwing erasers, you just flew under the radar. My teachers just wrote things on my report cards like "highly enthusiastic" or "needs to learn to wait her turn" or "a bit of a chatterbox." My parents just thought I was a tomboy with a lot of energy who liked to get into things. So no, nobody ever pulled my folks aside and suggested there was an actual medical reason for why I couldn't sit still through a single family dinner. It just wasn't something people talked about back then, especially not for girls who were otherwise doing okay.

And as for a family history... well, if anyone in my family had anything like this, they certainly never got an official label for it. We weren't really a "go to the doctor to talk about your brain" kind of family anyway. You just kept busy and got to work. 

Though, honestly, if I really sit back and think about it... my dad was a lot like me. He was a general contractor, and he was just always, always moving. He'd be juggling fifteen different job sites, talking a mile a minute to the subcontractors, constantly pacing. If my mom ever tried to make him sit down and watch a movie with us on a Friday night, he'd be up pacing the back of the living room by the second act, or suddenly deciding he needed to go reorganize the garage at nine o'clock at night. But he was never diagnosed with anything! He was just... you know, considered a "hard worker" with a lot of drive. That's just how we all framed it. 

So, officially? No. No history on paper, no past diagnoses for me. This is all completely new territory, which is probably why it's so incredibly frustrating trying to unpack it all now at this stage in my career. I've just always thought this was just who I am, just my personality, you know?

Distracted? By things around me? Um... no, actually. I don't think so. I know it probably seems like I would be, right? I don't suddenly forget why I'm there and start watching the guy do his yard work. 

Even back at the office, it's the same thing. If I'm tearing through those banker boxes I mentioned earlier, or if I'm drafting up a final case report for a client, the phone could be ringing off the hook, the junior detectives could be arguing about lunch orders right outside my door, the copier could be jamming and beeping that annoying high-pitched error tone, and I just tune it all out completely. I just zero in on whatever project I've decided needs my attention right that second. 

So no, I wouldn't say I get distracted easily. It's more like... I have this incredibly intense, laser-like focus, but the laser just happens to be attached to a motor that absolutely refuses to shut off, if that makes sense? Like, my body always has to be doing something, I always have to have that forward momentum, but whatever task I'm actually tackling, I am completely and totally consumed by it. I don't lose my train of thought just because a bird flew past the window or someone dropped a pen. Because when you get a call that a subject is on the move and you have to tail them, you can't be running around your house looking for your gear. You just have to grab and go. My ex-husband used to joke that my brain might be loud, but my closets and filing cabinets were a work of art.

You would think so, right? Because I just told you how intensely I can focus on things. But honestly, no. It really doesn't decrease at all. The physical stuff just... finds a different outlet, I guess. 

Like, okay, let's say I'm deep into a complex corporate fraud case. I've got my airtight filing system all set up, and I'm stuck at the computer for hours, just combing through hundreds of pages of bank records, wire transfers, offshore shell company filings... really dense, high-concentration stuff. My brain is totally locked in. But my body? My body absolutely refuses to get the memo that we are supposed to be sitting still. 

Under the desk, my foot is just going a mile a minute. Just bouncing, bouncing, bouncing, like I'm stepping on an invisible gas pedal. And my hands—if I'm not actively typing, I have to be doing something with them. Usually, I'm clicking a pen. Just constantly clicking it open and closed. It drives the junior investigators absolutely up the wall if they have to be in the room with me while I'm doing it.

I'll sit cross-legged, then I'll drop one foot to the floor, then I'll lean all the way back, then I'll hunch forward over the keyboard. Because, like I said, I'm trying to focus on these complex financial trails, and suddenly I have to re-read the exact same paragraph about a Cayman Islands holding company three times because my body decided it needed to do a gymnastics routine in my ergonomic office chair. 

It's not like I'm doing it on purpose, either. I don't even realize I'm doing half of it until someone points it out, or until my leg actually starts cramping up from bouncing so hard. It's like the more mental energy I have to expend on a task, the more physical energy just leaks out of my extremities. I remember this one time I was doing a deep-dive skip-trace, just staring at utility bills on my monitor for literally four hours straight, and by the time I finally found the address discrepancy I was looking for, I realized the carpet under my desk was practically worn down from my shoe rubbing against it the entire time. 

So, no, the restlessness definitely doesn't go away just because my brain is engaged. It's just always there, humming in the background, making me bounce around my desk while I'm trying to work.

Waiting for my turn? Oh, gosh. Yes. Yes, definitely. It is... well, it’s actually a huge problem for me, to be completely honest. I mean, waiting in general is just agonizing, but in conversations? It's like a physical pain in my chest if I have to hold a thought in. 

Like, okay, I was just talking about the junior investigators, right? So, we have these morning briefings every Monday. And the lead investigator—who, frankly, talks incredibly slowly, like he's savoring every single syllable—will be going over a case file. And I know exactly where he's going with it. I can see the conclusion three steps ahead. He'll be saying, "Well, the subject was seen at the marina, and we know he has a boat..." and I just cannot stop myself. I'll just blurt out, "So we need to pull the harbor master's logs and check the fuel receipts, right, I'll get on that." And he just stops and glares at me. And I know I shouldn't do it! I know it's rude. I tell myself before every meeting, "Just bite your tongue, let him finish his sentence." But it's like... the words just bubble up my throat and out of my mouth before my brain can even hit the brakes. 

And it’s not just at work, either. It’s in everyday life. My friends get so annoyed with me. We'll be at dinner, and someone will be telling a story, and I’ll just jump right in the middle of it. Sometimes I’m trying to finish their sentence for them because they’re taking too long to get to the point, or sometimes they say one little thing that sparks a thought in my head, and I just have to get it out right that second, or I feel like I'll explode. I literally interrupted my sister at her own wedding rehearsal dinner. She was giving this heartfelt toast, and she paused to take a breath, and I just launched into this whole tangential story about the caterer. I still feel terrible about it. She was furious. 

And lines? Oh my god, don't even get me started on waiting in lines. The grocery store, the DMV, even just waiting for the coffee machine at the office. I can't just stand there. I'm shifting my weight, I'm sighing out loud, I'm looking at my watch, I'm checking my phone, I'm literally pacing in place. If there are more than three people in front of me at the grocery checkout, I will just abandon my cart and leave. I can't do it. The feeling of being trapped in a queue, just waiting for other people to take their turn... it makes my skin crawl. It's like every second stretches out into an hour. So, yeah, waiting my turn, whether it's to speak or to do something... it's a massive struggle. It always has been.
